question: A 24-year-old woman presents with oligomenorrhoea (cycles every 35–45 days) and ultrasound showing 13 follicles per ovary each measuring 2–9 mm (polycystic ovarian morphology). Serum testosterone is at the upper limit of normal and there are no clinical features of hirsutism. Using the Rotterdam 2003 criteria, which of the following best applies?

answers.text: PCOS cannot be diagnosed because there are no clinical or biochemical signs of androgen excess

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is incorrect. Rotterdam 2003 requires any 2 of the 3 criteria: (1) oligo/anovulation, (2) clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, (3) polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound. This patient satisfies criteria 1 and 3, which is sufficient.

answers.text: PCOS can be diagnosed because the patient satisfies 2 of the 3 Rotterdam criteria: oligo-anovulation and polycystic ovarian morphology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Rotterdam 2003 requires any 2 of 3 features. Oligo-anovulation (cycles 35–45 days) + polycystic ovarian morphology (≥12 follicles, or updated 2018 threshold ≥20 follicles on modern ultrasound) = PCOS, provided secondary causes are excluded.

answers.text: PCOS requires all 3 Rotterdam criteria to be present simultaneously

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is a common misconception. Rotterdam 2003 criteria require ANY 2 of the 3 features, not all 3. All 3 together represent just one phenotype (the most complete) but are not required for diagnosis.

answers.text: PCOS can only be diagnosed if a DHEA-S level is elevated, confirming adrenal androgen excess

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: DHEA-S elevation points toward adrenal origin (CAH, adrenal tumour) and would actually prompt exclusion of adrenal pathology rather than confirming PCOS. PCOS is a diagnosis of exclusion that does not require adrenal androgen elevation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Rotterdam 2003 = ANY 2 of 3: (1) oligo/anovulation, (2) clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, (3) polycystic ovarian morphology. Oligo-anovulation + PCOM = PCOS (once secondary causes excluded). All 3 are NOT required.
Excellent. The Rotterdam 2003 rule is 2 of 3 — this is one of the highest-yield facts in PCOS and appears repeatedly in examinations.
